query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: If friction stir processing is applied to create a nanocrystalline surface layer in CoCrFeNi, followed by a brief pre-oxidation heat treatment, then a stable oxide-rich tribofilm will form and maintain a lower coefficient of friction (<0.3) and reduced wear rates from 25 to 800 °C compared to an untreated, coarse-grained alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy in an as-received, coarse-grained condition.
generation.intervention: Localized friction stir processing of the surface (≈50 μm thick) to achieve submicron grain size, followed by a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (600–700 °C) in air.
generation.conditions: Sliding contact tests in air across 25–800 °C under moderate normal loads (e.g., 10–100 N).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanocrystalline-grained surface layer plus oxide scale formed during pre-oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Surface nanocrystallization enhances the formation and stability of protective oxide tribofilms, reducing frictional shear and wear throughout the test temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significantly lower friction (below 0.3) and reduced wear rate compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi material under the same loads and temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi material in coarse-grained condition tested under identical tribological conditions.
generation.boundary: Effective for 25–800 °C sliding in air at moderate normal loads. The performance in more aggressive environments or substantially higher loads remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Exact friction and wear reductions are not fully established; the process may require further refinement or composition tuning for extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two CoCrFeNi samples: one with friction stir-processed and pre-oxidized surface, another in the as-received condition. Conduct pin-on-disk or ball-on-disk sliding tests in air from 25 °C to 800 °C at normal loads ranging from 10 N to 100 N. Measure friction coefficient and wear volume after each test.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature and load
Wear rate or specific wear volume via profilometry
Characterization of the worn surface by SEM to assess tribofilm formation and microstructure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the friction stir-processed sample fails to maintain an appreciably lower coefficient of friction or wear rate than the as-received alloy under these conditions, the hypothesis is disproven.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

decision.trend: Starting with CoCrFeMnNi alloys tested in vacuum (PMC7311485, 2020), researchers noted that grain refinement could improve wear resistance by promoting a stable, ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayer. Next (PMC8470387, 2021), adding W to AlCoCrFeNi coatings enhanced high-temperature wear performance via lattice distortion and second-phase strengthening, suggesting that controlled phase evolution is beneficial for hot-wear resistance. More recently, studies on CoCrFeMnNi under varied loads (PMC9960858, 2023) again confirmed that finer grain sizes reduce friction and wear. Another multi-principal-element alloy (PMC10241162, 2023) demonstrated ultralow wear from room temperature to 800 °C by activating an adaptable, multi-phase friction interface—implying that stable microstructures and protective tribofilms are key across wide temperature ranges. Despite such progress, a fundamental, direct solution for consistent low friction and wear in CoCrFeNi from ambient to 800 °C remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: It is still not clear how to achieve the same kind of thermally robust tribofilm and microstructural self-adaptation in CoCrFeNi, while avoiding the pitfalls of composition changes and ensuring that friction and wear remain low over drastic variations in temperature, load, and environment. The interplay between surface modifications, microstructure, and tribo-oxidation pathways has not yet been established for this specific alloy over the full 25–800 °C range.
decision.lever: Apply localized friction stir processing to create a nanocrystalline-grained surface layer (e.g., ~50 μm thick, grain size <500 nm) in CoCrFeNi, followed by a light oxide-stabilizing pre-oxidation heat treatment (e.g., 600–700 °C in controlled atmosphere).
decision.why: Studies on CoCrFe(Mn)Ni showed that stable, ultra-fine near-surface microstructures and in situ tribofilms reduce friction and wear. Introducing such a layer via friction stir processing can promote uniform surface nanocrystallization and facilitate the formation of a robust high-temperature oxide layer. This approach should maintain low friction (<0.3) and wear rates across the target 25–800 °C range, even under different loads and in air, by combining the beneficial effects of grain refinement and stable tribo-oxides. A controlled experiment would compare friction-stir-processed and as-received CoCrFeNi using identical tribotests from room temperature to 800 °C. If no significant improvement in friction and wear over the baseline alloy is observed under these conditions, the hypothesis would be falsified.
